blocks.text: A 38-year-old woman has lost 8 kg in three months despite eating well, her heart races at rest, and her eyes look prominent. Her blood shows an undetectable TSH. By contrast, a man on long-term prednisolone for polymyalgia stops it abruptly, develops vomiting, dizziness and a blood pressure of 78/45, and no one realises that his adrenal glands have switched off. The endocrine axes work on feedback, and every result must be read against the hormone above it.

blocks.markdown: Most endocrine systems are controlled by an **axis**: the hypothalamus releases a releasing hormone, the pituitary releases a tropic hormone (TSH, ACTH, LH/FSH, GH, prolactin), and the peripheral gland releases its hormone, which feeds back negatively. For the thyroid, TRH stimulates TSH, which stimulates thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3); for the adrenal, CRH stimulates ACTH, which stimulates cortisol. This means that in **primary** disease (the gland fails) the pituitary hormone moves in the opposite direction to the gland hormone, while in **secondary** disease (the pituitary or hypothalamus fails) they move in the same direction.

rows: Graves disease (TSH receptor antibodies, diffuse goitre, eye disease), toxic nodule, thyroiditis
Hashimoto thyroiditis (anti-TPO antibodies), after thyroid surgery or radioiodine, iodine deficiency

blocks.title: Reading thyroid function tests
blocks.prompt: A 52-year-old woman has tiredness, weight gain, constipation and cold intolerance. TSH is 24 mU/L (reference about 0.4 to 4.0) and free T4 is 7 pmol/L (reference about 12 to 22). Interpret the results and name the likely cause and treatment.

steps.text: Free T4 is low, so thyroid hormone is deficient.
TSH is high, so the pituitary is responding appropriately to low thyroid hormone. High TSH with low T4 is primary hypothyroidism.
In an adult woman in an iodine-sufficient region, autoimmune Hashimoto thyroiditis is the commonest cause; anti-TPO antibodies support it.
Treatment is replacement with levothyroxine, adjusting the dose by TSH after about 6 to 8 weeks.

blocks.answer: Primary hypothyroidism, most likely autoimmune; treat with levothyroxine.

items: Hyperthyroidism features: weight loss with good appetite, heat intolerance, palpitations or atrial fibrillation, tremor, diarrhoea, anxiety, lid lag. Graves disease adds eye signs and pretibial myxoedema.
Treatment: beta-blocker for symptoms; antithyroid drugs (carbimazole), which can cause agranulocytosis so patients are warned to report sore throat or fever; radioiodine; surgery.
Hypothyroidism features: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, slow reflexes.
Levothyroxine replacement is dosed by body weight (teaching example: about 1.6 micrograms/kg/day for full replacement in a healthy adult) and monitored by TSH.

blocks.markdown: **Cushing syndrome and adrenal insufficiency.** The adrenal cortex makes cortisol (zona fasciculata), aldosterone (zona glomerulosa) and androgens. **Cushing syndrome** is cortisol excess. The commonest cause is exogenous glucocorticoid therapy; endogenous causes are ACTH-dependent (pituitary adenoma, called Cushing disease, or ectopic ACTH from, for example, small cell lung cancer) and ACTH-independent (adrenal adenoma or carcinoma). Features: central obesity, moon face, dorsal fat pad, purple striae, thin skin and easy bruising, proximal myopathy, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis, mood change. **Investigation:** first confirm hypercortisolism with an overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol fails to suppress), 24-hour urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol; then measure ACTH to find the source and image accordingly. **Adrenal insufficiency** is cortisol deficiency, and in primary disease (Addison disease, most often autoimmune) aldosterone is also lost: fatigue, weight loss, postural hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and hyperpigmentation (from high ACTH, which shares a precursor with melanocyte-stimulating hormone). In secondary disease (pituitary failure or withdrawal of steroids) there is no hyperpigmentation and potassium is usually normal because aldosterone is preserved. Diagnosis: low early-morning cortisol and an inadequate response to the short Synacthen (ACTH) test. **Adrenal crisis** is treated immediately with IV hydrocortisone (teaching example 100 mg) and IV saline, without waiting for tests.

rows: Central obesity, moon face, striae, bruising

blocks.title: Is the patient on enough steroid to suppress the axis?
blocks.prompt: A patient takes prednisolone 10 mg daily. Equivalent doses are: prednisolone 5 mg, hydrocortisone 20 mg, dexamethasone 0.75 mg. Calculate the hydrocortisone-equivalent dose and comment on the risk.

steps.text: Set up the ratio: 5 mg prednisolone corresponds to 20 mg hydrocortisone.

40 mg hydrocortisone is well above normal physiological production (about 15 to 25 mg per day), so after weeks of this dose the axis is suppressed. Doses should be tapered rather than stopped abruptly, and extra cover is needed during acute illness.

blocks.answer: Hydrocortisone-equivalent 40 mg/day: suppression likely; taper, do not stop abruptly.

blocks.markdown: **Pituitary tumours** present in two ways: by **mass effect** (headache; bitemporal hemianopia from upward compression of the optic chiasm, classically starting in the upper temporal quadrants; cranial nerve palsies if the tumour invades the cavernous sinus; hypopituitarism from compression of normal pituitary) and by **hormone secretion**. Tumours smaller than 10 mm are microadenomas and larger ones macroadenomas. Prolactinoma (commonest) causes galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea or infertility in women and erectile dysfunction in men, and is treated first-line with a dopamine agonist such as cabergoline. Growth hormone excess causes acromegaly (large hands and feet, coarse features, sweating, carpal tunnel, hypertension, diabetes), diagnosed by failure of growth hormone to suppress in an oral glucose tolerance test and raised IGF-1. ACTH excess causes Cushing disease. Surgery (transsphenoidal) is used for most tumours except prolactinomas.

blocks.title: Read the axis
blocks.text: Always interpret the pituitary hormone and the end-organ hormone together. Opposite directions suggest primary gland disease; same direction suggests pituitary or hypothalamic disease.

points: In primary thyroid disease TSH and free T4 move in opposite directions; in central disease they move together (low T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH).

Cushing syndrome is confirmed biochemically (dexamethasone suppression, urinary free cortisol) before localising; adrenal insufficiency is diagnosed by low cortisol and inadequate Synacthen response, and adrenal crisis needs immediate hydrocortisone and saline.
Pituitary tumours present by mass effect (bitemporal hemianopia, hypopituitarism) or hormone excess (prolactin, growth hormone, ACTH); prolactinomas are treated first with a dopamine agonist.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has palpitations, new atrial fibrillation and weight loss. He has a firm, palpable thyroid nodule, no eye signs and no antibodies. TSH is below 0.01 mU/L and free T4 is 34 pmol/L. A radioisotope scan shows uptake in the nodule only, with suppressed uptake in the rest of the gland. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: suppressed TSH, high T4 and focal uptake in a single nodule.
distractorRationale.b: Hashimoto thyroiditis causes hypothyroidism with a high TSH.
distractorRationale.d: Subclinical hypothyroidism has high TSH with normal T4.

questions.explanation: A suppressed TSH with raised free T4 shows primary thyroid overactivity. Uptake confined to one nodule with suppression of the rest of the gland indicates an autonomously functioning adenoma rather than Graves disease, which gives diffuse uptake and eye signs.

questions.stem: After removal of a pituitary macroadenoma, a patient has fatigue and cold intolerance. TSH is 0.9 mU/L (reference 0.4 to 4.0) and free T4 is 8 pmol/L (reference 12 to 22). How should these results be interpreted?

options.text: Central hypothyroidism, because TSH is inappropriately normal for a low T4

questions.correctOptionText: Central hypothyroidism, because TSH is inappropriately normal for a low T4

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a low T4 should drive the TSH up, so a normal TSH means the pituitary is failing.
distractorRationale.b: Primary hypothyroidism would have a high TSH.

questions.explanation: With a healthy pituitary, a low free T4 provokes a high TSH. A normal TSH with low T4 after pituitary surgery shows loss of the feedback response, so the other pituitary axes must be tested, and adrenal insufficiency excluded or treated before thyroxine is started.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has weight gain with central obesity, purple abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness and hypertension. She takes no medications. What is the most appropriate first-line screening test?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: failure of cortisol to suppress confirms hypercortisolism.
distractorRationale.c: The Synacthen test tests for adrenal insufficiency.
distractorRationale.d: Prolactin is not the screen for Cushing syndrome.

questions.explanation: The picture suggests Cushing syndrome after exclusion of exogenous steroid. Dexamethasone normally suppresses ACTH and cortisol, and failure to suppress cortisol indicates autonomous production, after which ACTH is measured to find the source.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has fatigue, weight loss, postural dizziness, pigmentation of palmar creases and buccal mucosa, sodium 124 mmol/L, potassium 6.1 mmol/L and glucose 3.3 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary failure

distractorRationale.a: Correct: loss of cortisol and aldosterone with raised ACTH causes pigmentation, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia.
distractorRationale.b: Secondary disease has no pigmentation and normal potassium.
distractorRationale.c: Cushing syndrome has hypertension and hyperglycaemia.
distractorRationale.d: Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalaemia.

questions.explanation: Pigmentation indicates high ACTH, which occurs only when the adrenal itself fails, and hyperkalaemia shows aldosterone loss. Treatment in a crisis is immediate IV hydrocortisone and saline, with the diagnosis confirmed by cortisol and Synacthen testing.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has a 3-month history of headaches and bumping into objects on both sides. Visual fields show bitemporal hemianopia, worse in the upper quadrants. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm from below

questions.correctOptionText: Pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm from below

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the chiasm carries crossing nasal retinal fibres from both eyes, which are compressed from below first.
distractorRationale.d: Graves eye disease causes proptosis and diplopia.

questions.explanation: The optic chiasm lies just above the pituitary fossa, so an expanding macroadenoma presses on the decussating fibres that carry the temporal visual fields, giving bitemporal hemianopia that starts in the upper quadrants. This is a mass effect indication for imaging and for pituitary hormone testing.

questions.stem: As a pharmacology teaching example, full levothyroxine replacement in a healthy adult is about 1.6 micrograms/kg/day. Calculate the dose in micrograms per day for a 75 kg adult.
questions.explanation: 1.6 micrograms/kg x 75 kg = 120 micrograms per day. In practice older patients and those with heart disease start low and the dose is titrated against TSH after 6 to 8 weeks.

questions.stem: A patient has taken prednisolone 12.5 mg daily for 2 months. Using the equivalence prednisolone 5 mg = hydrocortisone 20 mg, calculate the hydrocortisone-equivalent daily dose in mg.
questions.explanation: 12.5 / 5 x 20 = 50 mg hydrocortisone per day, about double physiological production, which explains why the HPA axis is suppressed. Such a patient needs a gradual taper and stress cover for illness, to avoid adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: Explain how TSH and free T4 are interpreted in primary hyperthyroidism, primary hypothyroidism, subclinical hypothyroidism and central hypothyroidism, using the principle of negative feedback.
markingGuide: Negative feedback: thyroid hormone suppresses TSH
Primary hyperthyroidism: low TSH, high free T4 or T3
Primary hypothyroidism: high TSH, low free T4
Subclinical hypothyroidism: high TSH, normal free T4
Central hypothyroidism: low or inappropriately normal TSH with low free T4
Examples of causes: Graves disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis, pituitary disease
Treatments: antithyroid drug or radioiodine; levothyroxine
questions.explanation: In primary thyroid disease the pituitary responds appropriately, so TSH moves opposite to T4. In central disease the pituitary itself fails, so TSH is low or normal despite low thyroid hormone.

questions.stem: Compare the clinical features and investigation of Cushing syndrome and primary adrenal insufficiency, including the emergency treatment of adrenal crisis.
markingGuide: Cushing: central obesity, moon face, striae, bruising, proximal myopathy, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis
Causes of Cushing: exogenous steroids, pituitary adenoma, ectopic ACTH, adrenal tumour
Cushing tests: overnight dexamethasone suppression, 24 h urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol, then ACTH
Adrenal insufficiency: fatigue, weight loss, postural hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, pigmentation in primary disease
Tests: early-morning cortisol and short Synacthen test
Adrenal crisis: IV hydrocortisone and IV saline immediately, without waiting for tests
Secondary disease: no pigmentation, normal potassium
questions.explanation: Cushing syndrome is cortisol excess and adrenal insufficiency is cortisol deficiency, so their features are largely opposite. Adrenal crisis is lethal if untreated, so treatment is given before confirmatory tests.

questions.stem: True or false: the first-line treatment for a small prolactinoma causing galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea is transsphenoidal surgery.
questions.explanation: Prolactinomas respond to dopamine agonists such as cabergoline, which lower prolactin and shrink the tumour, so medical therapy is first-line. Surgery is reserved for intolerance or resistance and for most other pituitary adenomas.
